noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand the basic principles of a mass spectrometer and be able to analyse and interpret mass spectra to: i deduce the isotopic composition of a sample of an element ii calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from relative abundances of isotopes and vice versa iii determine the relative molecular mass of a molecule, and hence identify molecules in a sample iv understand that ions in a mass spectrometer may have a 2+ charge
be able to predict mass spectra, including relative peak heights, for diatomic molecules, including chlorine, given the isotopic abundances

primer.text: The mass spectrometer is the census-taker of isotopes. This note follows a sample through ionisation, acceleration, deflection and detection, averages isotope abundances into relative atomic masses, extends the technique to molecular ions and the carbon-13 M+1 satellite, and predicts the telltale halogen doublets and triplets.

lessons.title: Reading a mass spectrum of an element
lessons.opening: The mass spectrometer is the instrument that finds what balances cannot: the mass and abundance of each isotope. This lesson walks a sample through vaporisation, ionisation, acceleration, deflection and detection, then reads the spectrum the detector prints.
keyPoints: A mass spectrometer determines relative isotopic masses and their relative abundances.
Electron bombardment vaporises the sample and knocks electrons out, making positive ions.
Electromagnets in the flight tube deflect ions by their mass-to-charge ratio.
Every detector strike is recorded as a small current and amplified into a peak.

low.restatement: The machine turns atoms into positive ions, bends their paths by mass, and counts how many of each mass arrive.
low.analogy: It is a sorting chute for ions: heavier loads curve less and land at their own bin, each hit ringing the bell.
low.examPointer: Sequence marks come from naming the five stages in order.

medium.restatement: Ionisation converts neutral atoms into charged particles so fields can act on them; varying the magnetic field sweeps every mass-to-charge ratio across the detector, and abundance follows from strike frequency.
medium.analogy: Charging the balls is what lets the magnet sort them - uncharged marbles ignore the field entirely.
medium.examPointer: Applications beyond isotopes - drug detection, forensics, space probes and carbon dating - earn naming marks.

check.stem: What does a mass spectrometer determine for a sample of an element?

options.text: The relative isotopic mass and relative abundance of each isotope
options.explanation: The two outputs the instrument is built for.

options.text: The number of covalent bonds in the sample
options.explanation: Bonding is not what the instrument reads.

options.text: The boiling point of each isotope
options.explanation: Physical properties like boiling point are out of scope.

options.text: The electron configuration of the atoms
options.explanation: Configurations come from ionisation-energy data, not the spectrometer.

check.stem: Why must the sample be ionised inside the spectrometer?

options.text: Fields can only accelerate and deflect charged particles
options.explanation: Neutral atoms ignore electric and magnetic fields, so no sorting occurs.
Vaporisation happens first, as a separate stage.
No radioactivity is involved.
Ionisation removes electrons, slightly reducing mass.

check.stem: What role do the electromagnets around the flight tube play?

options.text: They deflect the ions' paths into curves whose radius depends on mass-to-charge ratio
options.explanation: The field sorts ions by how readily their momentum curves.
Ionisation is done by the electron gun.
The detector plate, not the magnets, registers strikes.
Temperature control is not the magnets' job.

check.stem: What does the detector record for each ion strike?

options.text: A small current, which is then amplified
options.explanation: Each strike registers electrically and the signal builds the spectrum.

options.text: A flash of light whose colour is measured
options.explanation: The detection is electrical, not optical.
Temperature is not the detected quantity.
The output is an electronic spectrum, not a print.

check.stem: Varying the electric and magnetic fields makes which deflection outcome possible?

options.text: All charged particles, whatever their mass-to-charge ratio, can be swept onto the detector
options.explanation: Sweeping the fields reads out the whole isotopic population.

options.text: The sample is reheated between readings
options.explanation: Vaporisation happens once.
Field variation does not change charges.
The geometry is fixed.

check.stem: State the five stages a sample passes through in a mass spectrometer.
check.modelAnswer: Injection and vaporisation, electron-bombardment ionisation, acceleration toward negative plates, deflection in the flight tube's electromagnetic field, and detection as amplified current.

check.stem: State two applications of mass spectrometry beyond isotope analysis.
check.modelAnswer: Detecting illegal drugs and supporting forensic science are two; space exploration and carbon-14 dating are further examples.

check.stem: Explain why the spectrometer reports mass-to-charge ratio rather than mass alone.
check.modelAnswer: The deflection a field produces depends on both how heavy the ion is and how many charges it carries - a doubly-charged ion curves like a lighter singly-charged one - so the field sort naturally reads the ratio m/z; for singly-charged molecular ions the ratio still equals the relative mass.

check.stem: In the flight tube, why do lighter singly-charged ions of the same charge deflect MORE than heavier ones at fixed field strength?
check.modelAnswer: Deflection depends on the mass-to-charge ratio: with equal charge, a lighter ion carries less momentum for the same field to bend, so its path curves more sharply toward the detector.

lessons.title: From abundances to relative atomic mass
lessons.opening: A spectrum is a census of isotopes, and the census averages into the periodic table's Ar values. This lesson applies the weighted-mean equation to oxygen and boron spectra, then extends the technique to molecular ions and the M+1 carbon-13 peak.
keyPoints: Isotopes are same-element atoms with equal protons but different neutron counts.
Ar = (abundance x mass summed over isotopes) / 100.
The molecular ion (M+) peak's m/z equals the compound's relative molecular mass; the M+1 peak grows with carbon count.

low.restatement: Multiply each isotope's mass by its abundance, add them up, divide by 100 - that weighted average is the Ar.
low.analogy: It is a class average where each isotope's mark is weighted by how many students (atoms) earned it.
low.examPointer: Read abundances straight off the peak heights when a spectrum is drawn.

medium.restatement: The weighted mean converts an isotopic mixture into one effective mass per atom; for molecules, the M+ peak reports the molecular mass while the M+1 satellite reports carbon-13's natural abundance, scaling with carbon count.
medium.analogy: The M+ peak is the molecule's weight, and the M+1 peak is the shadow it casts because one carbon in a hundred is heavier.
medium.examPointer: m/z 58 identifies propanal over butanal (72) - molecular-ion peaks distinguish candidates.

check.stem: What defines isotopes of one element?

options.text: Equal protons and electrons, different neutron counts
options.explanation: The element stays the same while the neutron count varies.
Different protons would mean different elements.
Neutral isotopes share electron arrangements.
Isotopes of a neutral element carry no charge difference.

check.stem: A sample holds 99.76% oxygen-16, 0.04% oxygen-17 and 0.20% oxygen-18. What is Ar to 2 dp?

options.explanation: The trace isotopes cannot shift the mean that far.
That reads the middle isotope's mass as the average.
The arithmetic sign of the trace correction was flipped.

check.stem: Why does boron's mass spectrum show peaks at masses 10 and 11 in ratio about 20:80?

options.text: Boron has two isotopes, B-10 and B-11, with those natural abundances
options.explanation: Peak positions give masses; peak heights give abundances.

options.text: Because boron forms B2 molecules in the machine
options.explanation: Element spectra here read atomic ions.
Neither isotope is radioactive.

options.text: Because the 10 peak is an M+1 satellite
options.explanation: Both are isotope peaks, not carbon-13 satellites.

check.stem: What information does the M+ peak of a molecular spectrum carry?

options.text: The compound's relative molecular mass, because m/z there equals Mr
options.explanation: The highest-mass peak is the whole molecule with one electron removed.

options.text: The number of carbon atoms present
options.explanation: That is the M+1 peak's information.
Unrelated to the spectrum.
That is the base peak, a different feature.

check.stem: Hexane's carbon-13 M+1 peak stands taller than ethane's. Why?

options.text: Hexane has six carbons to ethane's two, and each carbon adds a chance of being carbon-13
options.explanation: The M+1 height scales with carbon count.
Volatility is irrelevant.
Ionisation is single-electron here.

options.text: Because ethane has no carbon-13 at all
options.explanation: Carbon-13 exists at ~1% in every organic compound.

check.stem: State the weighted-mean equation for relative atomic mass from isotopic data.
check.modelAnswer: Ar = (abundance of isotope 1 x its mass + abundance of isotope 2 x its mass + ...) / 100.

check.stem: State the relative atomic mass of boron from its 19.9% / 80.1% spectrum.
Explain why a spectrum can identify propanal rather than butanal.
check.modelAnswer: The molecular ion peak sits at the compound's relative molecular mass: propanal's CH3CH2CHO+ ion reads m/z 58 while butanal's extra CH2 pushes its molecular ion to 72, so the observed M+ position discriminates the two candidates.

check.stem: Use the weighted-mean equation to show that boron's Ar is 10.8, given 19.9% B-10 and 80.1% B-11.

lessons.title: Predicting halogen doublets
lessons.opening: Chlorine and bromine wear their isotopes openly, printing unmistakable peak patterns into molecular spectra. This lesson builds the 3:1, 9:6:1, 1:1 and 1:2:1 patterns from probability and reads them as element detectors.
keyPoints: Chlorine: 35Cl and 37Cl in 3:1 ratio give M : M+2 peaks at 3:1 for one Cl atom.
Two chlorine atoms give three peaks in 9:6:1 ratio from (3/4, 1/4) pairing.
Bromine: 79Br and 81Br in 1:1 ratio give equal M and M+2 peaks for one Br atom.
Two bromine atoms give a 1:2:1 triplet; halogens are therefore visible in spectra.

low.restatement: One chlorine atom splits a molecular ion into a 3:1 doublet; one bromine atom makes an even 1:1 doublet.
low.analogy: The halogen tag is like a barcode printed on the spectrum: count the bars and you know which halogen and how many atoms.
low.examPointer: Quote the abundance ratio (3:1 or 1:1) before quoting peak ratios - the logic marks live there.

medium.restatement: Each halogen atom contributes an independent 3/4-1/4 (chlorine) or 1/2-1/2 (bromine) probability, so two atoms multiply: (3/4)^2 : 2(3/4)(1/4) : (1/4)^2 = 9:6:1 for chlorine and 1:2:1 for bromine.
medium.analogy: It is coin-toss arithmetic: two coins make HH, HT+TH, HT patterns with 1:2:1 counts - bromine is a fair coin, chlorine a biased one.
medium.examPointer: The M+2 peak's doubled weight for mixed isotopes (two ways to make 35-37) is the step examiners watch for.

check.stem: A compound containing ONE chlorine atom shows what molecular-ion pattern?

options.text: Two peaks, M and M+2, in a 3:1 height ratio
options.explanation: 35Cl gives M and 37Cl gives M+2, matching the isotope abundance.
That needs TWO chlorine atoms.
Two isotopes guarantee two peaks.
That is bromine's signature.

check.stem: Where does the 9:6:1 ratio in a two-chlorine compound come from?

options.text: The probabilities (3/4)(3/4), 2 x (3/4)(1/4) and (1/4)(1/4) for the three isotope pairings
options.explanation: Each atom is an independent 3:1 draw.

options.text: The three peaks' masses add those numbers
options.explanation: The ratio is probabilistic, not arithmetic on masses.
Isotopes do not react with each other.
Fields sort, they do not scale heights.

check.stem: Why does the M+2 peak double in height for the mixed 35Cl-37Cl pairing in two-chlorine compounds?

options.text: The mixed pair can form two ways - 35 then 37, or 37 then 35 - and both land at the same mass
options.explanation: Two routes to one peak double its height.
Its abundance is one third of 35Cl's.

options.text: Because the detector counts it twice
options.explanation: Counting is physical, not double-booked.
They are exactly 2 mass units heavier.

check.stem: A compound with one bromine atom shows what pattern?

options.text: M and M+2 peaks of EQUAL height
options.explanation: 79Br and 81Br are equally abundant.
That is chlorine's ratio.
That needs two chlorines.
Two isotopes guarantee the doublet.

check.stem: Bromine's two-atom molecules give a 1:2:1 triplet. What molecular logic underlies the middle peak?

options.text: 79Br-81Br and 81Br-79Br both land at M+2, combining to double height
options.explanation: Symmetrically, both mixed pairings weigh the same.
The abundances are equal.

options.text: The middle peak is a fragment, not a molecular ion
options.explanation: It is the genuine M+2 molecular ion.
One compound, three isotope combinations.

check.stem: State the peak patterns for molecules containing one and two chlorine atoms.
check.modelAnswer: One chlorine: M and M+2 peaks in 3:1 ratio. Two chlorines: M, M+2 and M+4 peaks in 9:6:1 ratio.

check.stem: State the isotope pair and abundance ratio for bromine.
check.modelAnswer: Bromine exists as 79Br and 81Br in roughly equal abundance, so single-Br compounds show 1:1 M / M+2 peaks.

check.stem: Explain why halogen-containing compounds are so easy to spot in mass spectra.
check.modelAnswer: No common organic element else produces these fingerprints: chlorine's 3:1 (or 9:6:1) and bromine's 1:1 (or 1:2:1) molecular-ion doublets and triplets arise directly from the isotopes' natural abundances, so the pattern itself names the halogen and counts its atoms.

check.stem: Predict the molecular-ion peak pattern, with ratio, for a compound containing two chlorine atoms.
check.modelAnswer: Three peaks: M (35-35), M+2 (mixed) and M+4 (37-37) in the ratio 9:6:1, from (3/4)^2, 2 x (3/4)(1/4) and (1/4)^2.

glossary.definition: The mass of one isotope relative to carbon-12, measured by the mass spectrometer.
The percentage share of an isotope in a natural sample, read from peak heights.
The whole molecule with one electron removed, whose m/z equals the relative molecular mass.
The satellite peak from carbon-13's natural abundance, growing with the molecule's carbon count.

workedExample.prompt: Boron's mass spectrum shows peaks at m/z 10 (19.9%) and m/z 11 (80.1%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron to 1 dp.
